eligibility.exact_action_basis: The candidate whole H.R.3898 House EH is a26-section Clean Water Act and related permitting package, including the seven further amendments adopted under rule936, not the21-section RH alone. It would require State/EPA water-quality-standard attainment/cost and United States commercial-technology availability/scale considerations, including the defined combined-sewer-overflow review; require new/revised specified water-quality criteria by rule; and add domestic commercial availability/scale factors to the three specified effluent-guideline provisions. Section5 would confine401 certification to the specified direct-discharge/compliance determination and listed301/302/303/306/307 requirements, require reasons for denials/conditions, publicly identified application information and the printed30-/90-day information procedures, and a reasonable action period capped at one year after a complete written request. Individual versus general-license/permit request information differs. This changes the broader dated401(d) State-law/limitation language; it does not abolish certification. The added401(h) judicial regime is restricted to certification for interstate/foreign energy-transmission or fuel facilities OR FERC-license/permit applicants:30-day filing; applicant OR direct/irreparable-economic-harm plaintiff, with every organizational member satisfying that harm requirement;120-day decision plus up to60days for extraordinary circumstances; and denial with prejudice for missed court deadlines only where certification has been granted. It is not a universal Clean Water Act court rule. Section6 would require notice at least two years before general-permit expiry when EPA does not intend reissue, and continue old terms for previously or otherwise-covered discharges until reissue or two years after that notice, whichever first. Section7 changes the State-program402(b)(1)(B) fixed-term ceiling from five to ten years;402(a)(3) subjects federal permits to the same terms/conditions/requirements, so this is not a claim about every possible permit or an assertion that the federal cross-reference disappears. Section8 would expand the402 permit shield for identified/monitored pollutants or pollutants within identified waste streams/processes/operations and require a water-quality-based limitation to identify the pollutant and a numerical or narrative action/control level. Section9 adds the specified fire-retardant/water-enhancer discharges for forestry/fire suppression; section10 addresses precipitation-responsive agricultural stormwater, including subsurface drainage and qualified adjacent, functionally related and necessary support land. Section11 would exempt the defined FIFRA-authorized pesticide point-source discharges from402 permitting, with water-relevant FIFRA-violation/increased-discharge, regulated-stormwater and listed industrial/treatment/vessel exceptions. Section12 would confine EPA404(c) restrictions to the complete-application-to-permit-issuance interval for post-enactment applications. Section13 changes404 general-permit duration from five to ten years and specifies discharge-effect scope and minimal-effect tests, including under-three-acre treatment; three or more acres may still qualify as minimal. The defined nationwide linear-infrastructure under-three-acre discharge category is distinct from the linear-pipeline half-acre-or-less LOSS category. Nationwide reissuance receives the printed ESA-consultation and NEPA-assessment/EIS treatment, with preserved single/complete-project and GeneralCondition15 references; this is not a general waiver for every individual permit. Section14 requires a written additional State-program-information request within45days. Section15 sets60-day filing limits for the three specified404 decisions, with comment/issue exhaustion limited to the approval/issuance categories rather than the separate verification category; establishes remand without State-program vacatur; and restricts permit/discharge injunction or vacatur subject to the imminent/substantial-danger AND no-other-equitable-remedy exception. Its remand schedule is limited to180days except as law provides. New section16 would ratify the named Michigan, New Jersey and Florida404 programs and prevent withdrawal absent a later Act; permit dual Army/Florida issuance during the90-day transition; and require the specified approval determination for comparable State programs, followed by notifications and Army suspension when the State begins administration. These are proposed statutory changes to the retained404(g)–(i) framework, not certification of the programs’ current judicial status. Section17 requires the180-day State-program regulatory review and implementation of appropriate revisions. New section18 requires a PROPOSED mitigation-framework rule within180days, not a final rule by then; specified flexibility, regional credit/service areas, coordination and temporary-impact/reclamation treatment; recognition of existing financial assurances; and surplus-credit use/transfer/sale only with applicable environmental performance standards. Reclamation-plan categories retain their listed legal qualifications; objective success criteria and phased-release guidance follow the final rule. Section19 addresses the jurisdictional-determination/wetlands-delineation backlog outstanding June5,2025 through the specified60-day expedited/reallocated-resources requirement. Section20 adds navigable-water exclusions for the specified waste-treatment systems, direct-precipitation ephemeral features, groundwater and jointly determined features, and qualified prior-converted cropland with pre-December23,1985 and preceding-ten-year-use requirements plus the not-reverted-to-wetlands condition; it is not every agricultural wetland. Section21 changes the farm SPCC aggregate professional-certification threshold20,000→42,000gallons, allows the qualified owner-certification range strictly greater than10,000and less than42,000gallons and at-or-below10,000gallon/no-reportable-history exemption, while preserving the separate professional-engineer triggers for an individual tank above10,000gallons OR reportable oil-discharge history. It changes the separate-parcel container carve-out capacities1,000→1,320 and2,500→3,000gallons and removes the study/adjustment mechanism. It does NOT change the distinct1,000gallon/42gallon reportable-oil-discharge-history definition or the other unchanged aggregation exclusions. Section22 encourages rather than compels qualified States’ FAST coordination. Section23 is a sense of Congress on Chesapeake Bay, not a new binding permit standard. New section24 requires Army-land recharge-site identification in one year, qualified streamlined permitting and consultation to the extent practicable, and an18-month report; its literal section17 cross-reference is preserved without correction. New section25 establishes the voluntary State-led nitrogen/phosphorus-impaired-water pilot with voluntary agricultural-producer participation and no new nonpoint-source regulation or expanded federal jurisdiction. New section26 authorizes the United States section of IBWC to accept federal/nonfederal funds for the specified wastewater, conservation and flood-control work, deposited to the specified Treasury account and subject to available appropriations until expended. Its total five-million-dollar-per-fiscal-year restriction applies to nonfederal credit/reimbursement, not every project cost; the defined foreign-country-of-concern source/agreement prohibition and annual reporting remain. These are whole-package proposed legal mechanisms, not actual permits, construction, funding receipts, water-quality effects or enactment. The official Record deems the RH substitute adopted, records amendments1/2/3/4/6/7/8 agreed to with5not offered, then en-gros adoption and engrossment; the separate resumed vote rejects recommittal329 and passes330. The retained EH matches the reconstructed operative sections. This candidate evidence does not approve or apply the still-unresolved canonical whole-passage binding.

Clyde amendment1 to H.R.4776 would insert, after “final agency action” on printed RHpage26 line8, that the bill’s direct-harm condition shall not include aesthetic, recreational, or emotional interests unaccompanied by material physical or property harm. The target is the proposed NEPA section110B(c)(1)(C) requirement that the filing party has suffered or imminently will suffer direct harm from the final agency action. The unaccompanied condition matters: the amendment does not categorically exclude every claim involving those interests when material physical or property harm accompanies them. It changes that specific proposed bill clause, rather than all current-law standing. The surrounding150-day-or-shorter deadline, qualifying public-comment/same-subject conditions, categorical-exclusion-establishment bar and separate Tribal-trust-resources provisions are not deleted by this insertion. The Tribal provision’s exceptions for the beneficiary Tribe’s own challenges and reasonably foreseeable outside-trust effects remain distinct. An initial voice-aye announcement and postponed recorded demand were followed by roll352 rejection; the operative amendment did not enter the retained final EH.

Roy amendment5, offered as Perry’s designee, would replace printed RHpage5 lines15–18 in H.R.4776’s proposed NEPA section106(c)(1). It would allow consideration only of effects over which the lead agency OR cooperating Federal agencies have jurisdiction by law AND that share a reasonably close causal relationship to, AND are proximately caused by, the immediate project or action under consideration. Either the lead agency or cooperating Federal agencies may supply jurisdiction; the amendment does not require the lead agency alone or all agencies jointly to have it. The existing proposed RHclause already contains both causal qualifications; the added jurisdiction condition is an additional limit in that exact bill provision, not a claim that all current-law review already lacks such limits. Paragraph(c)(2)’s separate exclusions for speculative/attenuated, time/place-separated or separate-project effects are not struck. This amendment does not itself approve or deny a project or change the entire parent package. The preliminary voice-aye announcement was followed by postponed proceedings and roll353 rejection, leaving the added jurisdiction phrase absent from the retained final EH.

Roy amendment6 would add two linked provisions after printed RHpage23 line13. First, proposed NEPA section111, as amended by H.R.4776, would receive paragraph16 defining “significant effect on the quality of the human environment” as a proximate AND concrete harm directly caused by the proposed agency action that materially impairs human health OR property. Second, section102(2)(C) would replace “significantly affecting the quality of the human environment, a detailed statement” with “with at least one significant effect on the quality of the human environment, an environmental impact statement”. Both the new definition and its paired trigger replacement are the exact amendment choice; the property alternative is not an additional mandatory health requirement. The dated2024 operative section102(2)(C) contains the original significantly-affecting/detailed-statement text, and section106(b) separately governs EIS/assessment levels. This is a proposed statutory definition and trigger, not a finding that a specific action actually produces qualifying harm or escapes every review duty. It does not delete every other document, alternative or assessment requirement. The preliminary voice-aye result and postponement were followed by roll354 rejection; neither of these two edits appears in the retained final EH.

The candidate whole H.R.4776 House EH would add an express purely procedural/no-mandated-result NEPA statement; expand threshold circumstances where no environmental document is required when other statutory compliance, or qualified State/Tribal review with a lead-agency determination, serves NEPA’s function; and change the environmental-assessment trigger from “does not” to “is not likely to” have the specified significant effect, preserving the unknown-significance branch. It would retain the essential/reasonable-cost research exception while adding no duty to undertake new research after an application. Reviewable effects and the new reasonably-foreseeable definition require both reasonably close and proximate causation by the immediate project, excluding the specified speculative, attenuated, time/place-separated and separate-project effects. The rejected Roy amendment5 jurisdiction condition is not part of this EH. Completed environmental documents for applicant projects could not be altered absent a court order or written applicant agreement. Authorization interference receives listed court-order, material-breach/law-violation, fraud/concealment/misrepresentation, newly unconsidered specific immediate substantial proximate life/property/security/defense harm, or holder/project-sponsor-request exceptions, alongside “existing law”, a savings clause neither expanding nor limiting existing authority, feasible/as-appropriate clear-and-convincing evidence, scope/duration limits, notice and project-circuit review. Federal-agency petitions for vacatur/voluntary remand require holder or sponsor written consent. The no-action-negative presumption is limited to a beneficiary Tribe-initiated action on/directly affecting its trust resources with a considered no-action alternative. One lead-agency no-document threshold determination would prevent another agency preparing a document for that same proposed action. The bill revises lead/cooperating roles and applicant purpose/need, limits Federal cooperating comments to jurisdiction-by-law matters, and establishes application notification60-day and subsequent60-day level-of-review clocks with the printed additional-information alternative. Agencies receive21-day invitation/acceptance clocks and7-day convening; unidentified agencies receive qualified7-day invitation and14-day scheduling treatment. Final agency action is due30days after the impact statement/assessment, with schedules for other outstanding authorizations; this is not automatic project approval or a30-day total review deadline. Existing two-year EIS/one-year assessment review periods remain in the renumbered provisions; extensions require applicant approval, with the specified limitation and exceptions on sponsor deadline litigation. Other applicable-law reviews run concurrently pursuant to applicable law. Scientific/technical information timing uses the earlier application/notice-or-decision date; delay to await later information is barred, with the express APA public-comment-information qualification. Programmatic reliance changes five to ten years while retaining new-circumstances/information and later reevaluation qualifications; substantially-same actions/effects may use prior supervised reviews, while other actions require necessary modification/augmentation made public as a new document. The package adds Congress-enacted categorical exclusions, broad authorization definitions, qualified Federal-control/funding and prior-agency-review exclusions from major Federal action, specified Farm Service Agency loan exclusions, no funding-alone major-action finding, and “energy” to CEQ policy-recommendation duties. New judicial section110B requires substantial agency deference and no substitution of judgment on effects; for the specified APA706(2)(A) NEPA failure the only remedy is remand without vacatur/injunction, continuing final-agency-action effect and the printed180-day correction limits, including older orders. Claims face150days unless shorter law applies, the qualified substantive-unique/timely/same-subject comment condition, direct harm and categorical-exclusion-establishment bar. Tribal-trust-resource review restrictions retain beneficiary-Tribe and outside-effects exceptions. Supplemental review is limited to newly contained information; its deadline sentence literally says the deadline “shall be the date” of public agency action, without a repaired150-day formula. Courts have the stated record-filing60-day and judgment180-day clocks; appeals have60-day filing and180-day decision limits, with remand appeal rights. Literal section110B(e)’s107(g)(3) reference is preserved despite the bill’s deadline renumbering. Crucially, section4 exempts from the entire Act and its amendments agency actions for which, between January20,2025 and enactment, an agency filed a voluntary-remand motion OR otherwise reopened/reconsidered/initiated statutory corrective action, whether or not completed at enactment. RHsections1–3 exactly match EHsections1–3, and H.Res.953 sections4/5 deem this complete added section4 adopted under H.Res.951. The retained own recorded unit and Clerk report House passage; this candidate chain does not approve or apply the canonically unresolved whole-passage binding.
